claim: The learned cascade operates at approximately 35% laboratory utilization.
The learned cascade retains diagnostic sensitivity while limiting laboratory utilization.
The learned defer policy defines a sensitivity-versus-laboratory-utilization frontier.
Learned referral can be compared with risk-based, uncertainty-based, random, and oracle allocation policies.
Laboratory allocation and final diagnostic performance vary across clinically relevant subgroups.
Under-referral among true diabetes cases can differ across demographic and clinical subgroups.
The defer gate uses a feature profile that is not identical to the cheap-stage diabetes risk predictor.
The learned defer score can be evaluated as a value-of-information signal for identifying cases where laboratory testing changes the cheap-stage decision.
Integrated Gradient feature rankings are cross-checked using feature-ablation importance.
The principal conclusions are evaluated under feature-group ablation, additional missingness, alternative outcome definitions, budget changes, and alternative clinical cost assumptions.
Selected neural models are retrained under alternative laboratory-budget constraints to test whether results depend only on post-hoc thresholding.
The final analysis uses a temporal holdout, with 2017–2018 reserved for final testing.
